processing: As with other sheng pu-erh, large-leaf leaf is wok-fixed, rolled and sun-dried, then sold loose or pressed. No ripening step in this raw form.
harvest_season: Spring is the prized picking, as elsewhere in Yunnan; autumn tea is also made in the province.
appearance_dry: Typical of Yunnan sheng: long, dark green leaf with some silvery buds, loose or pressed.
appearance_liquor: Clear golden yellow when young, deepening with age as other sheng does.
appearance_wet: As with other large-leaf sheng, thick olive-green leaves.
taste_profile: Strong and clean rather than showy: a pure tea flavour and mountain character are what the region is praised for, with fruit and some bitterness in common descriptions.

brewing.notes: Usual young sheng approach: quick rinse, short first steeps, and back off if bitterness builds.

vintage_note: Sold like other sheng, by harvest year and increasingly by village, mostly young and at gentler prices than the famous Xishuangbanna and Lincang mountains. It is less often seen abroad, so aged examples are hard to find. Check that year and place are stated.
description:
Baoshan is the western edge of the pu-erh map, often counted as one of Yunnan's four production areas alongside Xishuangbanna, Lincang and Pu'er. Most drinkers meet it as an interesting, good-value side trip rather than a benchmark.

The method is the usual one for sheng, so the differences come from place. Old tea gardens are concentrated around Bawai in Tengchong and at Wenjiatang and Huangjiazhai in Changning, and the Gaoligong range holds a further old-tree resource.

The common verdict is that Baoshan tea does not outdo the other three regions on character, but has strength and a pure flavour worth seeking. Brew it as any young sheng: hot water and short steeps.

Label it carefully in your head, since a place name on the wrapper tells you the area and not the quality. Good sellers will name the county or village. A Changning or Tengchong tea side by side is a fine way to learn the region.
history:
Baoshan has old gardens with long-standing trees, and Huangjiazhai in Changning is reported to have trees over a thousand years old, each tagged and registered. Changning has also set out rules and an association for protecting old trees.

The region has only recently gained attention among pu-erh drinkers, and tea guides still class it as emerging, with much less written about it than about the southern mountains.
